summary: Sets out IETF policies on intellectual property rights such as patents in IETF technology, so working groups know about any IPR constraints on a proposal. It was replaced by RFC 8179.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3979 says who has to tell the IETF about patents and other legal rights over a proposal, when they have to say so, and what the IETF does with the information. The short version: the IETF does not judge whether a patent is valid, but it will not let a patent be used to shut a standard down without saying so.

questions: who must disclose patents in the ietf
subtitle: The rules that keep patent holders from holding up Internet standards, and make people say what they know.

tldr.problem: Working groups were increasingly having to deal with patent claims over the technology they were considering, and the rules in the IETF standards process were ambiguous enough to cause repeated argument.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC clarifies the policy: the IETF makes no judgement on whether a patent claim is valid, but anyone who knows of intellectual property covering the technology under discussion must disclose it, and the disclosure must name the specific document and the specific rights.
tldr.outcome: The RFC sets out how disclosures are made, what happens when one arrives, and what a working group may do with the information. It was a Best Current Practice, the RFC Editor index lists it as obsoleted by RFC 8179, and it was later updated by RFC 4879.

today: RFC 3979 is a March 2005 Best Current Practice, and the RFC Editor index lists it as obsoleted by RFC 8179. It was later updated by RFC 4879.

sections.title: The Terms the Policy Uses
sections.content:
An IETF Contribution is any submission to the IETF intended by the contributor for publication as all or part of an Internet-Draft or RFC, except for RFC Editor Contributions, and any statement made within the context of an IETF activity. Such statements include oral statements in IETF sessions and written and electronic communications made at any time or place, addressed to the IETF plenary session, to any IETF working group or portion of it, to the IESG or a member of it on behalf of the IESG, to the IAB or a member of it on behalf of the IAB, to any IETF mailing list, or to the RFC Editor or the Internet-Drafts function. Statements made outside an IETF session, mailing list or other function that are clearly not intended as input to an IETF activity are not IETF Contributions.

Internet-Drafts are the temporary documents used in the IETF and RFC Editor processes. They are posted on the IETF web site by the Secretariat and have a nominal maximum lifetime in the Secretariat's public directory of 6 months, after which they are removed, although Internet-Drafts are archived many places on the Internet and not all of those places remove expired drafts. Drafts under active consideration by the IESG are not removed until that consideration is complete, and an author can ask for the lifetime to be extended before it expires.

Two definitions do the most work in the policy. Reasonably and personally known means something an individual knows personally or, because of the job the individual holds, would reasonably be expected to know. The wording indicates that an organization cannot purposely keep an individual in the dark about patents or patent applications just to avoid the disclosure requirement, but it does not require a contributor or participant to perform a patent search.

Covers, or covered, means that a valid claim of a patent or a patent application in any jurisdiction, or a protected claim, or any other intellectual property right, would necessarily be infringed by exercising a right such as making, using, selling, importing, distributing or copying with respect to an Implementing Technology, which is a technology that implements an IETF specification or standard. A valid claim is a claim of any unexpired patent or patent application that has not been withdrawn, cancelled or disclaimed, nor held invalid by a court of competent jurisdiction in an unappealed or unappealable decision. Intellectual property rights mean patent, copyright, utility model, invention registration, database and data rights that may cover an Implementing Technology, wherever in the world they arise and whether from a registration, a renewal or an application.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy is about two things: what you are obliged to tell the IETF, and what the IETF will do with it. It applies to anything you say in a working group, a mailing list or a meeting, not just to a formal document.

sections.title: Why the IETF Has an IPR Policy
sections.content:
In the years since the IETF standards process was published, the exact intent of its section on IPR disclosures was the subject of vigorous debate within the IETF community, because it had become increasingly common for working groups to have to deal with claims of intellectual property rights such as patent rights over the technology under discussion. The aim of this document is to clarify the ambiguities that led to those debates and to amplify the policy, to clarify what the IETF is, or should be, doing.

Disclosures can come at any point in the standards process: before the first Internet-Draft has been submitted, prior to RFC publication, or after an RFC has been published and the working group has closed down. They can come from people submitting technical proposals as Internet-Drafts, on mailing lists or at meetings, from other people participating in the working group, or from third parties who find out that the work is going or has gone on. They can be based on granted patents or on patent applications, and in some cases can be disingenuous, made to affect the process rather than to inform it.

The standards process established three basic principles for dealing with claims of intellectual property rights. The IETF makes no determination about the validity of any particular IPR claim. Following normal processes, the IETF can decide to use technology for which IPR disclosures have been made, if it decides that such a use is warranted. And so that the working group and the rest of the IETF have the information needed to make an informed decision, all those contributing to the working group's discussions must disclose the existence of any IPR that the contributor or other participant believes covers, or may ultimately cover, the technology under discussion. That applies to contributors and to other participants, whether they contribute in person, by email or by other means, and it applies to all IPR of the participant, the participant's employer, sponsor, or others represented by the participant, that is reasonably and personally known to the participant. No patent search is required.

The document is not intended to modify the IETF's policy toward IPR, but to clarify and fill in procedural gaps. A companion document deals with rights in contributions, such as copyrights and trademarks, including the right of the IETF and its participants to publish and create derivative works. The memo is also not intended as legal advice.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule has three parts. The IETF does not rule on whether a patent is valid. The IETF may still adopt a technology that has patents attached to it. And everyone who talks about that technology in the IETF has to say what they know about patents over it.

sections.title: What the IETF Does When a Disclosure Arrives
sections.content:
When an intellectual property right is disclosed before publication as an RFC, with respect to any technology or specification described in a contribution made in the manner the document sets out, the RFC Editor must ensure that the document includes a note indicating the existence of such claimed rights in any RFC published from the contribution.

The IESG disclaims any responsibility for identifying the existence of, or for evaluating the applicability of, any IPR to any IETF technology, specification or standard, and takes no position on the validity or scope of any such claims. Where rights have been disclosed, the IETF Executive Director must request from the discloser a written assurance that, upon approval by the IESG for publication as RFCs of the relevant specification, all persons will be able to obtain the right to implement, use, distribute and exercise other rights with respect to the implementing technology under one of the licensing options set out in the document, unless such a statement has already been submitted. The working group proposing the use of the technology may assist the Executive Director in this effort.

The results of this procedure do not, by themselves, block publication of an IETF document or its advancement along the standards track. A working group may take the results into consideration when evaluating the technology, and the IESG may defer approval when a delay may help in obtaining such assurances. The results are recorded by the Executive Director and made available online.

The IESG will not make any explicit determination that an assurance of reasonable and non-discriminatory terms has been fulfilled in practice. Instead it applies the normal requirements for the advancement of Internet standards. If the two unrelated implementations required to advance from Proposed Standard to Draft Standard have been produced by different organizations, or if the significant implementation and successful operational experience required to advance from Draft Standard to Standard has been achieved, the IESG presumes that the terms are reasonable and to some degree non-discriminatory. This also applies where multiple implementers have concluded that no licensing is required, and the presumption may be challenged at any time, including during the Last-Call period.

IETF and RFC Editor documents must not contain any mention of specific IPR. All specific disclosures must be submitted as described in the disclosure section, because a reader could be misled into thinking that the IETF, the IESG or the RFC Editor has formed an opinion on the validity, enforceability or applicability of the rights, or that the disclosures in the document are the only ones the IETF has received. Readers should always refer to the online list of disclosures for a full picture.
sections.plainLanguage: When a disclosure arrives, the RFC Editor notes it in the document, the IESG stays out of the argument about whether the patent is valid, and the IETF asks the patent holder to promise that anyone implementing the standard will be able to get a licence. The promise does not have to be perfect, and it never blocks publication on its own.

sections.title: Who Must Disclose, and What a Disclosure Must Say
sections.content:
A contributor who reasonably and personally knows of IPR meeting the conditions of the policy, and who believes it covers or may ultimately cover their own contribution, or who knows their employer or sponsor may assert it against implementing technologies based on that contribution, must make a disclosure. This requirement includes contributions made by any means, including electronic or spoken comments, unless the comment is rejected from consideration before a disclosure could reasonably be submitted. There are no exceptions to this rule, and a discloser is asked to withdraw a previous disclosure if a revised contribution negates it, or to amend it if the revision substantially alters it.

Any individual participating in an IETF discussion who knows of such IPR covering a contribution made by another person, or which their employer or sponsor may assert against implementing technologies based on that contribution, must also make a disclosure. A participant's obligation is also satisfied if the IPR owner, or the participant's employer or sponsor, makes an appropriate disclosure instead. Someone who has information about IPR that may cover IETF contributions but is not required to disclose, for example because the rights are owned by another company, is encouraged to notify the IETF by email instead.

Timing matters, because working groups need as much information as they can while they evaluate alternative solutions. A disclosure for one's own contribution must be made as soon as reasonably possible after the contribution is published in an Internet-Draft, unless the required disclosure is already on file. A disclosure about someone else's contribution must be made as soon as reasonably possible after the contribution is published in an Internet-Draft or RFC. Participants who realize that a contribution will be or has been incorporated into a submission, or is seriously being discussed in a working group, are strongly encouraged to make at least a preliminary disclosure without waiting for the document to be posted.

A disclosure must list the numbers of any issued patents or published patent applications, or indicate that the claim is based on unpublished applications, and must list the specific document or activity affected, referenced by version number if it is an Internet-Draft. If the document has several parts and it is not reasonably apparent which part is alleged to be covered, the discloser should identify the sections. A disclosure made on the basis of a patent application may be asked for again later to say whether the application has been published, abandoned or granted, and a granted patent requires the patent number, with a description of any material difference in applicability.

A blanket statement of possible IPR on every contribution does not satisfy the requirement, and neither does a blanket willingness to licence all potential IPR under fair and non-discriminatory terms. The requirement is satisfied by a blanket statement of willingness to licence all potential IPR meeting the conditions of the policy, to implementers of an IETF specification, on a royalty-free basis, as long as any other terms and conditions are disclosed.

It is helpful, though not mandatory, for a disclosure to say how the rights would be licensed, so that working groups have the information during their deliberations. The options are a royalty-free and otherwise reasonable and non-discriminatory licence, a licence with reasonable and non-discriminatory terms including a reasonable royalty or other payment, or no need to obtain a licence from the rights holder at all. Disclosures are required for IPR owned directly or indirectly by the individual, their employer or sponsor, or that those persons otherwise have the right to license or assert.
sections.plainLanguage: You must disclose if you know of rights that cover the technology being discussed, whether the words are yours or someone else's, and you must name the document and the rights. A general promise to licence everything is not enough on its own.

sections.title: Choosing Between Technologies, and Failing to Disclose
sections.content:
Working groups generally prefer technologies with no known IPR claims, or, for technologies with claims against them, an offer of royalty-free licensing. But they have the discretion to adopt technology with a commitment of fair and non-discriminatory terms, or even with no licensing commitment, if they feel that the technology is superior enough to outweigh the potential cost of the licences.

Over the last few years the IETF has adopted stricter requirements for some security technologies. It has become common to have a mandatory-to-implement security technology in an IETF specification, so that there is at least one common security technology present in all implementations and it can be used in all cases. This does not stop a specification from including other security technologies whose use could be negotiated between implementations. An IETF consensus has developed that no mandatory-to-implement security technology can be specified unless it has no known IPR claims against it, or a royalty-free licence is available to implementers, unless there is a very good reason to do otherwise. That limitation does not extend to other security technologies in the same specification that are not listed as mandatory-to-implement.

Two further points matter. The absence of IPR disclosures is not the same as knowing that there will be no claims in the future, because people who are not involved in the IETF, or who discover relevant rights in their patent portfolios, can disclose at any time. And the validity and enforceability of any IPR may be challenged for legitimate reasons, so the mere existence of a disclosure should not be taken to mean that the rights are valid or enforceable, although a working group will take its own view of that in evaluating alternatives.

There are cases where individuals are not permitted by their employers, or by other factors, to disclose the existence or substance of patent applications or other IPR. Since disclosure is required for anyone submitting documents or participating in IETF discussions, a person who does not disclose IPR for this reason, or any other reason, must not contribute to or participate in IETF activities with respect to technologies that they reasonably and personally know to be covered by IPR which they will not disclose. Contributing to or participating in IETF discussions about a technology without making required disclosures is a violation of IETF process.
sections.plainLanguage: Working groups are allowed to pick a technology that carries patents, if they think it is the better one. What they may not do is pick it in the dark. If you cannot disclose, you cannot take part in that discussion.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo relates to IETF process, not to any particular technology. There are security considerations when adopting any technology, whether it is protected by intellectual property rights or not, and a working group should take those into account as one part of evaluating the technology, just as IPR is one part. But there are no known issues of security with the IPR procedures themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is about process, not about any protocol, so it has no security advice of its own beyond one point: security still has to be weighed when a group chooses a technology.

viz.caption: THE THREE PRINCIPLES OF THE IETF IPR POLICY

items.title: No validity judgement
items.text: The IETF makes no determination about the validity of any particular IPR claim.

items.title: Use is a group decision
items.text: Following normal processes, the IETF can decide to use technology for which disclosures have been made.

items.title: Disclosure
items.text: Everyone taking part in the discussion must disclose the IPR they know covers the technology, with no patent search required.

viz.caption: THE LICENSING OPTIONS A DISCLOSURE MAY DESCRIBE

cells: All persons will be able to obtain the right to implement, use and distribute under a royalty-free and otherwise reasonable and non-discriminatory license.
All persons will be able to obtain the right under a license with reasonable and non-discriminatory terms, including a reasonable royalty or other payment.
All persons will be able to implement, use and distribute without the need to obtain a license from the IPR holder.
